content: The quantity of each product required to maintain insecticidal effectiveness over a 1 m² wall for the entire transmission period of the targeted disease within one year must be determined. The financial subcommittee should calculate the costs of the various products based on this information. For long-lasting insecticidal nets (LNs), the comparison criteria could be the cost per median year of net life under local conditions of use. The tender committee will evaluate recommendations from the financial and technical subcommittees and integrate both technical and financial measures to arrive at a value for money estimate before awarding a contract. The evaluation process for the tender should not exceed four weeks. The award proposal must be submitted to a senior official not directly involved in the tender process for endorsement or to the donor for a no objection. The results should then be communicated to all bidders. A contract department will initiate the procurement contract. Decision-making criteria at all stages must be clear, justifiable, and objective, particularly during the evaluation and comparison of bids. If the tender committee rejects a recommendation to procure the most cost-effective product that meets the established criteria, the reasons for rejection must be clearly stated, endorsed by the committee, and documented. Quality control of pesticides is essential to minimize risks associated with their handling and use, as well as to ensure their efficacy and stability during storage. Poor-quality pesticides can lead to inadequate application, increased risks for users and the environment, ineffective control, and potential resistance development. WHO specifications for pesticides provide an international reference standard for regulatory or commercial purposes, preventing the trade of substandard products. These specifications define the essential chemical and physical properties related to a product's efficacy and risk of use. All public health pesticides offered for sale should meet WHO specifications, where available. In the absence of WHO specifications, other relevant internationally accepted or national specifications should be considered. Bidders must provide evidence that their products comply with the relevant specifications, including a certificate of analysis for each batch at the time of delivery. Independent quality control of the product must be determined through analysis by the procurement entity. Quality control involves selecting an independent certified or accredited laboratory, random sampling of appropriate samples, shipping samples to the selected laboratory, and quality control analysis and reporting by the laboratory. To ensure transparency, the sampling agent and laboratory must be independent of the supplier. Pre-shipment analysis ensures that the product meets relevant specifications before shipment, avoiding subsequent issues if the delivered product is of poor quality. Quality control upon arrival or after shipment may be required if product traceability cannot be guaranteed, if tampering is suspected, or if the product has been exposed to unacceptable shipping or storage conditions. The selected laboratory must be independent of the manufacturer or supplier and equipped with the necessary infrastructure, equipment, and human resources to perform physico-chemical analysis of pesticide samples. The laboratory should have a quality assurance system in place, adhering to ISO 17025 accreditation standards or OECD principles of good laboratory practice, to ensure traceability and provide accurate, reliable results. This includes designating a quality assurance manager, maintaining a quality assurance manual, writing standard operating procedures (SOPs) for all operations and equipment, validating analytical methods, verifying method performance during sample analysis, recording raw data, organizing management reviews, training personnel, archiving raw data, and preparing study plans, contracts, and comprehensive reports. Participation in proficiency tests or collaborative trials is highly recommended. The laboratory should have robust infrastructure, including separate facilities for different activities (e.g., sample receipt, preparation, chromatographic determination, reagent storage, and offices), appropriate work tables, and fume hoods. It must possess all necessary resources, including equipment for physico-chemical testing of pesticides according to CIPAC methods and WHO specifications, as well as certified analytical standards, reagents, and solvents. The laboratory should employ qualified scientists and technicians, provide regular training, and participate in workshops on modern analytical techniques such as gas chromatography and high-performance liquid chromatography. Training in quality assurance is also recommended. The laboratory must be competent in analytical methods for pesticide quality control, applying methods referenced in pesticide specifications exactly as described to obtain reliable results. Access to WHO specifications, guidelines on pesticide analysis, and CIPAC and AOAC methods is essential. Accreditation according to ISO 17025 through a national body is generally more suitable for official quality control laboratories than quality assurance schemes under good laboratory practice, which are mandatory for studies required for national registration in OECD countries. Guidelines on quality control of pesticide products for national laboratories provide general guidance for establishing or strengthening national pesticide quality control, regardless of whether the product is used for public health or agriculture. While the use of a product may differ, quality control schemes are similar, and laboratories analyzing products for both areas may achieve synergies and rational resource use. These guidelines focus on laboratories analyzing pesticide products to ensure data generated are of sufficiently high standards to withstand external scrutiny. Reference is also made to laboratories engaged in pre-registration testing of products. The guidelines extend beyond quality control in conducting specific analyses to encompass the full range of management in laboratory operations, including organization, staff procedures, and facilities. The WHO Collaborating Centre for Quality Control of Pesticides can be requested by procurement entities to perform quality control of pesticides they procure. Proper sampling involves collecting, preparing, and documenting samples, including sufficient pesticide quantities for laboratory analysis, shipping and transaction records, and acknowledgment of receipt of subsamples and relevant documents by the party from whom samples are taken. Guidelines on sampling for quality control of technical-grade active ingredients and formulated pesticide products are published in the FAO and WHO specifications manual. Topics include safety precautions, general sampling principles, preparation for sampling, monitoring pesticide package properties, and sampling for testing physical and chemical properties. Before sampling, an independent sampling officer should be selected, and appropriate logistical arrangements and sampling apparatus should be available. Clean equipment and containers must be used to avoid contamination and ensure satisfactory analysis. Sampling procedures for liquid and solid products in small volumes involve randomly selecting three whole packages from the same batch. For larger packages, subsampling is recommended to facilitate handling and avoid disposal issues after analysis. Samples must be thoroughly mixed before taking three subsamples, preferably stored in glass containers with Teflon or polyethylene-lined caps. Sampling procedures for long-lasting insecticidal nets (LNs) and other products involve randomly selecting three entire nets from the same batch. Sampling protocols for mosquito coils, vaporizing mats, liquid vaporizers, and aerosol dispensers are described in the FAO and WHO specifications manual. The amount taken for each subsample may vary depending on the required tests. Samples should be taken from original, unopened packages, and if multiple batches exist, samples should be taken from the predominant batch. Each batch should be tested for compliance with specifications, with the number of batches and samples per batch depending on the buyer's confidence level in product quality. For liquid formulations, at least one sample per batch should be tested.
